items.title: At Least One
items.question: In a group, 20 people like tea, 15 like coffee, and 10 like both. How many like at least one of the two?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 25. Adding the two groups double-counts the overlap, so subtract it once.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 25. Adding the counts plainly would count the shared people twice.
items.lessonContent:
Overlaps cause double counting.
Add the groups, then subtract the shared part.
Inclusion and exclusion handles overlaps.
Check the total against the maximum.

items.title: Tea Only
items.question: Of those who like tea or coffee, 20 like tea, 15 like coffee, and 10 like both. How many like tea alone?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 10. Removing the 10 who like both from the 20 tea drinkers leaves tea-only.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 10. Subtracting the overlap isolates those who like only the first item.
items.lessonContent:
Isolate a group by removing the overlap.
Only means excluding the shared part.
Subtract rather than add here.
Track which region you want.

items.title: Coffee Only
items.question: With 15 coffee drinkers and 10 who like both, how many like coffee but not tea?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 5. The coffee-only region is the coffee total minus the shared members.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. Failing to subtract the overlap inflates the exclusive group.
items.lessonContent:
Exclusive regions shrink by the overlap.
Subtract the shared part from each side.
Keep the regions distinct.
Check that the regions sum correctly.

items.title: Liking Neither
items.question: A class of 30 includes 20 tea drinkers and 15 coffee drinkers, with 10 liking both. How many like neither?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 5. The 25 who like at least one leave five of the thirty outside both.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. Subtract the union from the total to find those in neither group.
items.lessonContent:
The outside region is the remainder.
Union plus complement equals the whole.
Compute the union first.
Subtract from the total.

items.title: Two Subjects
items.question: Among 30 students, 18 study maths, 20 study science, and 12 study both. How many study at least one?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 26. Eighteen plus twenty minus twelve gives the union.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 26. The overlap must be removed once to avoid counting those students twice.
items.lessonContent:
Union equals the sum minus the overlap.
Apply the formula to two sets.
Check the result against the total.
Watch for inflated counts.

items.title: Maths Alone
items.question: With 18 maths students and 12 who study both maths and science, how many study maths only?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 6. The twelve dual students are removed from the eighteen maths students.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 6. Exclusive groups require subtracting the shared members.

Subtract the overlap for exclusive membership.
Only excludes the shared part.

items.title: Science Alone
items.question: If 20 study science and 12 study both, how many study science without maths?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 8. Removing the overlap from the science total leaves the exclusive group.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 8. Forgetting the dual students overstates the science-only count.

Exclusive means minus the shared members.

items.title: Neither Subject
items.question: In a class of 30 with 18 maths and 20 science students and 12 taking both, how many take neither?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 4. The union is 26, so four of the thirty fall outside both subjects.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Subtract the union from the total to find the outside group.
items.lessonContent:
The complement is the leftover.
Find the union first, then subtract.
Every element is in or out.

items.title: Counting Rule
items.question: What is the name of the principle that adds set sizes and subtracts their overlaps to count a union?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The principle corrects the double counting caused by overlaps.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is inclusion and exclusion. It works for any number of sets by alternating additions and subtractions of overlaps.
items.lessonContent:
A named rule compresses a repeated correction.
Add memberships, remove overlaps.
Alternate for higher numbers of sets.
Use the formula to avoid ad hoc counting.

items.title: Readers Together
items.question: Of 40 people, 25 read newspaper A, 20 read newspaper B, and 10 read both. How many read at least one?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 35. Twenty-five plus twenty minus ten gives the union.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 35. The shared readers are counted twice unless the overlap is subtracted once.
items.lessonContent:
Overlap correction applies to any two groups.
Sum then subtract the shared part.
Check against the total population.
Avoid double counting.

items.title: Only A Readers
items.question: With 25 readers of A and 10 reading both papers, how many read only A?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 15. The ten dual readers are removed from the twenty-five.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 15. Exclusive readerships require subtracting the shared readers.

Remove the overlap for exclusivity.

items.title: Cyclists Only
items.question: A survey finds twenty cyclists, ten of whom also drive. How many cycle without driving?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 10. Subtracting the shared readers from the B total gives the exclusive group.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 10. Failing to subtract the ten who also drive inflates the exclusive count.

Exclusive counts shrink by the overlap.

items.title: Readers of Neither
items.question: Of 40 people, 35 read at least one of two papers. How many read neither?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 5. The outside group is the population minus the union.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. Complement counts always subtract the union from the whole.
items.lessonContent:
Outside equals whole minus union.
Complement work is a subtraction.

items.title: No Overlap
items.question: Two groups have sizes seven and nine and share no members at all. How many are in their union?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 16. With no overlap, the union is simply the sum of the two sizes.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 16. Disjoint sets require no correction, so the sizes add directly.
items.lessonContent:
Disjoint sets need no subtraction.
Add directly when nothing is shared.
Confirm the sets really are disjoint.

items.title: One Inside Another
items.question: If every member of set A is also in set B, how large is the union of A and B?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. When one set lies inside another, the union is just the larger set.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the size of B. The nested set adds nothing new to the union.
items.lessonContent:
Nesting simplifies unions.
The larger set absorbs the smaller.
Check containment before adding.

items.title: One Inside, Overlap
items.question: Set P contains every element of set Q. How many elements do the two have in common?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. When one set lies inside another, everything shared is the inner set itself.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the size of Q. The nested set contributes all of its members to the overlap.
items.lessonContent:
Nesting makes the smaller set the overlap.

items.title: Outside a Set
items.question: A set has four members within a universe of ten. How many things lie outside it?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 6. The complement is the universe minus the set.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 6. Subtracting the members from the universe gives those outside.
items.lessonContent:
The outside is a remainder.
Subtract membership from the universe.

items.title: Exactly One Sport
items.question: Of 50 students, 30 play football, 25 play cricket, and 10 play both. How many play exactly one of the two?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 35. The union is 45, and removing the 10 who play both leaves those in exactly one.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 35. Exactly one means the union minus the overlap, which excludes the dual players.
items.lessonContent:
Exactly one excludes the overlap.
Find the union, then subtract the shared members.
Distinguish at least one from exactly one.
Read the wording closely.

items.title: Neither Sport
items.question: In a club of fifty members, forty-five joined at least one of two activities. How many joined neither?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 5. The union is 45, leaving five outside both sports.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. Subtract the union from the population to find the outside group.
items.lessonContent:
Outside is the population minus the union.

items.title: Three Sets Union
items.question: Three sets each have ten members, every pair shares four, and all three share two. How many members are in the union?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 20. Adding the three sizes, subtracting the three overlaps, and adding back the triple gives twenty.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 20. The triple overlap must be added back after the pairwise subtractions.
items.lessonContent:
Alternate adding and subtracting overlaps.
The triple overlap is corrected last.
Follow the pattern for any number of sets.

items.title: In Exactly Two
items.question: With pairwise overlaps of four and a triple overlap of two, how many members lie in exactly two of the three sets?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 6. Each pairwise region minus the triple gives two, and there are three such regions.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 6. The triple members belong to three sets, so they must be removed from each pairwise count.
items.lessonContent:
Regional counts exclude higher-order overlaps.
Subtract the triple from each pair.
Multiply by the number of pair regions.
Keep regions mutually exclusive.

items.title: In Exactly One
items.question: Three sets each hold ten members, every pair overlaps in four, and the triple overlaps in two. Count the members belonging to just one set.
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 12. Each exclusive region holds four, and there are three such regions.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 12. Removing both the pairwise and triple overlaps from each set leaves the exclusive members.
items.lessonContent:
Exclusive regions require removing all overlaps.
Work set by set.
Subtract pairwise and triple contributions.
Then multiply by the number of sets.

items.title: Subsets of Five
items.question: How many subsets does a set with five elements have?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 32. Each element is either included or not, giving two to the fifth options.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 32. The count doubles with each added element because each one has two choices.
items.lessonContent:
Each element is in or out.
Independent choices multiply.
Powers of two count subsets.
Include the empty and full sets.

items.title: Subsets of Four
items.question: A set of four items — how many different selections can be formed from it, including none at all and all four?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 16. Four independent in-or-out choices give two to the fourth.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 16. Remember that the empty set and the whole set both count.
items.lessonContent:
Choices multiply when independent.
Add one element and double the count.

items.title: Why Subtract
items.question: Why must the shared members be subtracted when adding the sizes of two overlapping groups?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Anything shared sits in both counts, so it is tallied twice before the correction.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is double-counted elements. The subtraction removes exactly the extra tally caused by the overlap.
items.lessonContent:
Counting can repeat the same item.
Overlaps create extra tallies.
Correct by subtracting once.
Track what has been counted.
